# Fields with underscores can only be set by typing the underscore

## What happens now
When I declare a field whose name has a leading or a trailing underscore, the setup method that the library writes for me accepts only the name with the underscores still attached. So every time I build the object, I have to type the underscore in the keyword myself.

## What should happen
I should be able to pass the value under the plain name, with the surrounding underscores left off, whether they sit at the start of the field name, at the end, or at both ends. The field on the object should still carry its full underscored name, and the printed form should still show the underscores.

## About this project
This is a small library for Python that writes simple data classes for you. You list your fields on a few lines, and the library gives you a setup method, a readable printed form, comparisons, and value checks, so you do not write that repetitive code by hand.

## Problem this solves
Today every place that creates the object has to repeat the underscores, which is noisy and easy to slip up on. Letting me drop them at the call site makes building the object read like ordinary code and keeps the naming of my fields to one place.

## What changed
The setup method the library writes now takes each field under the name with leading and trailing underscores removed. Fields that have a plain value, a made-on-demand value, or a value check are all set through that same short name. Nothing was taken away: the stored field and the printed form keep the underscored name, and field names written without any underscores behave exactly as they did before.

## Impact
Ease of use at the call site. Stored values and printed output stay the same, and existing field names without underscores are untouched.

## User experience
Before: I declare a field whose name starts with an underscore, and the only way to build the object is to pass the same underscored keyword, so every call site carries the underscore along. After: I pass the plain short name when I build the object, the value lands on the underscored field, and the object still prints with its underscored name.

  17 │     *Read-only* representation of an attribute.
  18 │ 
  19 │     :attribute name: The name of the attribute.

  21 │     :attribute default_factory: see :func:`attr.ib`

  26 │         self.default_value = default_value
  27 │         self.default_factory = default_factory
  28 │         self.validator = validator

  30 │     @classmethod
  31 │     def from_counting_attr(cl, name, ca):

  33 │             name=name,

  35 │             default_factory=ca.default_factory,

  42 │       for name in ("name", "default_value", "default_factory", "validator")]
  43 │ Attribute = _add_cmp(_add_repr(Attribute, attrs=_a), attrs=_a)

  46 │ class _CountingAttr(object):
  47 │     __attrs_attrs__ = [
  48 │         Attribute(name=name, default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING,
  49 │                   validator=None)
  50 │         for name
  51 │         in ("counter", "default_value", "default_factory",)
  52 │     ]
  53 │     counter = 0

  55 │     def __init__(self, default_value, default_factory, validator):
  56 │         _CountingAttr.counter += 1

  58 │         self.default_value = default_value
  59 │         self.default_factory = default_factory
  60 │         self.validator = validator

  66 │ def _make_attr(default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING, validator=None):
  67 │     """
  68 │     Create a new attribute on a class.
  69 │ 
  70 │     .. warning::
  71 │ 
  72 │         Does nothing unless the class is also decorated with :func:`attr.s`!
  73 │ 
  74 │     :param default_value: Value that is used if an ``attrs``-generated
  75 │         ``__init__`` is used and no value is passed while instantiating.
  76 │     :type default_value: Any value.
  77 │ 
  78 │     :param default_factory: :func:`callable` that is called to obtain
  79 │         a default value if an ``attrs``-generated ``__init__`` is used and no
  80 │         value is passed while instantiating.
  81 │     :type default_factory: callable
  82 │ 
  83 │     :param validator: :func:`callable` that is called within
  84 │         ``attrs``-generated ``__init__`` methods with the :class:`Attribute` as
  85 │         the first parameter and the passed value as the second parameter.
  86 │ 
  87 │         The return value is *not* inspected so the validator has to throw an
  88 │         exception itself.
  89 │     :type validator: callable
  90 │     """
  91 │     if default_value is not NOTHING and default_factory is not NOTHING:
  92 │         raise ValueError(
  93 │             "Specifying both default_value and default_factory is "
  94 │             "ambiguous."
  95 │         )
  96 │ 
  97 │     return _CountingAttr(
  98 │         default_value=default_value,
  99 │         default_factory=default_factory,
 100 │         validator=validator,
 101 │     )

 104 │ def _get_attrs(cl):
 105 │     """
 106 │     Return list of tuples of `(name, _Attr)`.
 107 │     """
 108 │     attrs = []
 109 │ 
 110 │     for name, instance in sorted((
 111 │             (n, i) for n, i in cl.__dict__.items()
 112 │             if isinstance(i, _CountingAttr)
 113 │     ), key=lambda e: e[1].counter):
 114 │         attrs.append((name, instance))

 119 │ def _add_methods(maybe_cl=None, add_repr=True, add_cmp=True, add_hash=True,
 120 │                  add_init=True):
 121 │     """
 122 │     A class decorator that adds `dunder
 123 │     <https://wiki.python.org/moin/DunderAlias>`_\ -methods according to the
 124 │     specified attributes using :func:`attr.ib`.
 125 │ 
 126 │     :param add_repr: Create a ``__repr__`` method with a human readable
 127 │         represantation of ``attrs`` attributes..
 128 │     :type add_repr: bool
 129 │ 
 130 │     :param add_cmp: Create ``__eq__``, ``__ne__``, ``__lt__``, ``__le__``,
 131 │         ``__gt__``, and ``__ge__`` methods that compare the class as if it were
 132 │         a tuple of its ``attrs`` attributes.  But the attributes are *only*
 133 │         compared, if the type of both classes is *identical*!
 134 │     :type add_cmp: bool
 135 │ 
 136 │     :param add_hash: Add a ``__hash__`` method that returns the :func:`hash` of
 137 │         a tuple of all ``attrs`` attribute values.
 138 │     :type add_hash: bool
 139 │ 
 140 │     :param add_init: Add a ``__init__`` method that initialiazes the ``attrs``
 141 │         attributes.
 142 │     :type add_init: bool
 143 │     """
 144 │     # attrs_or class type depends on the usage of the decorator.  It's a class
 145 │     # if it's used as `@_add_methods` but ``None`` (or a value passed) if used
 146 │     # as `@_add_methods()`.
 147 │     if isinstance(maybe_cl, type):
 148 │         cl = maybe_cl
 149 │         cl.__attrs_attrs__ = []
 150 │         # Replace internal `_CountingAttr`s with `Attribute`s.
 151 │         for name, ca in _get_attrs(cl):
 152 │             a = Attribute.from_counting_attr(name=name, ca=ca)
 153 │             cl.__attrs_attrs__.append(a)
 154 │             setattr(cl, name, a)
 155 │         return _add_init(_add_hash(_add_cmp(_add_repr(cl))))
 156 │     else:
 157 │         def wrap(cl):
 158 │             cl.__attrs_attrs__ = [
 159 │                 Attribute.from_counting_attr(name=name, ca=ca)
 160 │                 for name, ca in _get_attrs(cl)
 161 │             ]
 162 │             if add_repr is True:
 163 │                 cl = _add_repr(cl)
 164 │             if add_cmp is True:
 165 │                 cl = _add_cmp(cl)
 166 │             if add_hash is True:
 167 │                 cl = _add_hash(cl)
 168 │             if add_init is True:
 169 │                 cl = _add_init(cl)
 170 │             return cl
 171 │ 
 172 │         return wrap

1 │ .. _examples:
   2 │ 
   3 │ Examples
   4 │ ========
   5 │ 
   6 │ The simplest possible usage would be:
   7 │ 
   8 │ .. doctest::
   9 │ 
  10 │    >>> import attr
  11 │    >>> @attr.s
  12 │    ... class Empty(object):
  13 │    ...     pass
  14 │    >>> Empty()
  15 │    Empty()
  16 │    >>> Empty() == Empty()
  17 │    True
  18 │    >>> Empty() is Empty()
  19 │    False
  20 │ 
  21 │ So in other words: ``attrs`` useful even without actual attributes!
  22 │ 
  23 │ But you'll usually want some data on your classes, so let's add some:
  24 │ 
  25 │ .. doctest::
  26 │ 
  27 │    >>> @attr.s
  28 │    ... class Coordinates(object):
  29 │    ...     x = attr.ib()
  30 │    ...     y = attr.ib()
  31 │ 
  32 │ These by default, all features are added, so you have immediately a fully functional data class with a nice ``repr`` string and comparison methods.
  33 │ 
  34 │ .. doctest::
  35 │ 
  36 │    >>> c1 = Coordinates(1, 2)
  37 │    >>> c1
  38 │    Coordinates(x=1, y=2)
  39 │    >>> c2 = Coordinates(x=2, y=1)
  40 │    >>> c2
  41 │    Coordinates(x=2, y=1)
  42 │    >>> c1 == c2
  43 │    False
  44 │ 
  45 │ As shown, the generated ``__init__`` method allows both for positional and keyword arguments.
  46 │ 
  47 │ If playful naming turns you off, ``attrs`` comes with no-nonsense aliases:
  48 │ 
  49 │ .. doctest::
  50 │ 
  51 │    >>> @attr.attributes
  52 │    ... class SeriousCoordinates(object):
  53 │    ...     x = attr.attr()
  54 │    ...     y = attr.attr()
  55 │    >>> SeriousCoordinates(1, 2)
  56 │    SeriousCoordinates(x=1, y=2)
  57 │    >>> attr.ls(Coordinates) == attr.ls(SeriousCoordinates)
  58 │    True
  59 │ 
  60 │ 
  61 │ Sometimes you want to have default values for your initializer.
  62 │ And sometimes you even want mutable objects as default values (ever used accidentally ``def f(arg=[])``?).
  63 │ ``attrs`` has you covered in both cases:
  64 │ 
  65 │ .. doctest::
  66 │ 
  67 │    >>> import collections
  68 │    >>> @attr.s
  69 │    ... class Connection(object):
  70 │    ...     socket = attr.ib()
  71 │    ...     @classmethod
  72 │    ...     def connect(cl, db_string):
  73 │    ...        # connect somehow to db_string
  74 │    ...        return cl(socket=42)
  75 │    >>> @attr.s
  76 │    ... class ConnectionPool(object):
  77 │    ...     db_string = attr.ib()
  78 │    ...     pool = attr.ib(default_factory=collections.deque)
  79 │    ...     debug = attr.ib(default_value=False)
  80 │    ...     def get_connection(self):
  81 │    ...         try:
  82 │    ...             return self.pool.pop()
  83 │    ...         except IndexError:
  84 │    ...             if self.debug:
  85 │    ...                 print "New connection!"
  86 │    ...             return Connection.connect(self.db_string)
  87 │    ...     def free_connection(self, conn):
  88 │    ...         if self.debug:
  89 │    ...             print "Connection returned!"
  90 │    ...         self.pool.appendleft(conn)
  91 │    ...
  92 │    >>> cp = ConnectionPool("postgres://localhost")
  93 │    >>> cp
  94 │    ConnectionPool(db_string='postgres://localhost', pool=deque([]), debug=False)
  95 │    >>> conn = cp.get_connection()
  96 │    >>> conn
  97 │    Connection(socket=42)
  98 │    >>> cp.free_connection(conn)
  99 │    >>> cp
 100 │    ConnectionPool(db_string='postgres://localhost', pool=deque([Connection(socket=42)]), debug=False)
 101 │ 
 102 │ More information on why class methods for constructing objects are awesome can be found in this insightful `blog post <http://as.ynchrono.us/2014/12/asynchronous-object-initialization.html>`_.

 104 │ 
 105 │ Although your initializers should be a dumb as possible, it can come handy to do some kind of validation on the arguments.
 106 │ That's when :func:`attr.ib`\ ’s ``validator`` argument comes into play.
 107 │ A validator is simply a callable that takes two arguments: the attribute that it's validating and the value that is passed for it.
 108 │ If the value does not pass the validator's standards, it just raises an appropriate exception:
 109 │ 
 110 │ .. doctest::
 111 │ 
 112 │    >>> def smaller_than_5(attribute, value):
 113 │    ...     if value >= 5:
 114 │    ...         raise ValueError("'{name}' has to be smaller than 5!"
 115 │    ...                          .format(name=attribute.name))
 116 │    >>> @attr.s
 117 │    ... class C(object):
 118 │    ...     x = attr.ib(validator=smaller_than_5)
 119 │    >>> C(42)

 121 │       ...
 122 │    ValueError: 'x' has to be smaller than 5!

 125 │

 127 │ 
 128 │    >>> @attr.s
 129 │    ... class C(object):
 130 │    ...     x = attr.ib(validator=attr.validators.instance_of(int))
